name: Secretin
evidenceNote: Synthetic human secretin has held FDA approval since 2004 for three diagnostic jobs: measuring pancreatic output, checking for gastrinoma, and guiding endoscopy. It is used once, during a test, rather than as an ongoing treatment.
summary: Secretin is the gut hormone that triggers bicarbonate release from the pancreas. Its synthetic form (ChiRhoStim) is FDA-approved for diagnostic tests.
keyTakeaway: Secretin is a 27-amino-acid hormone released by the small intestine when stomach acid arrives, signaling the pancreas to pour out bicarbonate-rich fluid. Its 1902 discovery gave medicine the idea of a hormone. A synthetic copy, ChiRhoStim, has been FDA-approved since 2004 to test pancreatic function, help diagnose gastrinoma, and help locate pancreatic duct openings during endoscopy. Side effects are rare: 9 of 531 trial patients had nausea. In the late 1990s it was promoted for autism, but 16 randomized trials found no benefit.

blocks.text: Secretin is a peptide hormone made in the lining of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. When acid, fat or protein from the stomach reaches the duodenum, secretin is released into the blood and travels to the pancreas, telling it to send out fluid rich in bicarbonate, the same chemical as baking soda, which neutralizes stomach acid [1].

The drug version, ChiRhoStim, is synthetic human secretin with an amino acid sequence identical to the natural 27-amino-acid hormone [1]. It is not used to treat disease. Doctors give it during specialized tests to see how well the pancreas works, to look for a hormone-producing tumor called a gastrinoma, and to help find the pancreatic duct openings during endoscopy [1].

Secretin holds a special place in medical history. Writing in 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling published their work on how the pancreas is told to secrete [3]. They showed the signal from the intestine travels as a chemical in the blood rather than along nerves, and named the substance secretin [2][3].

Within three years that finding had grown into the general concept of the hormone, and secretin is regarded as the first substance identified as one [9]. Over the following century it was purified, its structure worked out, chemically synthesized, and its receptor identified and cloned [2].

items.text: Bayliss and Starling describe a blood-borne signal from the intestine that drives pancreatic secretion [3].
A randomized trial in 60 children finds a single dose of synthetic secretin does not help autism [5].
FDA approves ChiRhoStim, synthetic human secretin, as a new molecular entity under priority review [7].
A Cochrane review of 16 trials concludes secretin is not an effective autism treatment [6].

blocks.text: Secretin binds secretin receptors on the cells that line the pancreatic ducts. That opens CFTR channels, the same chloride channels that are faulty in cystic fibrosis, and the cells release large volumes of bicarbonate-rich fluid. Nerve pathways through the vagus nerve also seem to take part, since blocking them blunts the response [1].

This predictable response is what makes it useful in testing. When secretin is injected and the fluid draining from the pancreas is collected, low volume or low bicarbonate points to a pancreas that is not working well. In people with a gastrinoma, secretin paradoxically makes the tumor release more gastrin, a hormone that drives acid production, which helps confirm the diagnosis [1]. Synthetic human secretin has an elimination half-life of about 45 minutes [1].

Yes. FDA approved ChiRhoStim on April 9, 2004, as a new molecular entity under priority review, and it remains a prescription product in two vial strengths [7]. It is given only by intravenous injection in a clinical setting [1].

Earlier products were made from pig secretin, including a synthetic porcine version called SecreFlo that FDA approved in 2002 and that is now listed as discontinued [8]. The approved uses of synthetic human secretin are diagnostic only. Promotion of secretin as a treatment for autism in the late 1990s never led to an approval, and later trials found no benefit [5][6].
ChiRhoStim is approved to stimulate secretions for three diagnostic purposes [1]:

items: Testing exocrine pancreatic function, the pancreas's output of digestive fluid and bicarbonate, in conditions such as chronic pancreatitis [1]
Helping diagnose gastrinoma, by measuring how much gastrin rises after injection [1]

Making the ampulla of Vater and the accessory papilla, where the pancreatic ducts drain, easier to find during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), a procedure that examines the bile and pancreatic ducts [1]

blocks.text: Secretin has also been studied as an aid to MRI. In a phase 3 trial of 258 people with pancreatitis, adding synthetic human secretin to magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), an MRI scan of the ducts, let radiologists detect duct abnormalities with significantly higher sensitivity than standard MRCP, using ERCP as the reference [4]. That imaging use is not part of the ChiRhoStim label [1].

Side effects are uncommon. In an open-label trial of 531 patients aged 1 to 91, most given a single dose, the most frequent reactions were nausea in 9 people, vomiting in 3, and flushing and upset stomach in 2 each. The label lists no contraindications [1].

The main cautions concern test accuracy rather than safety. People with alcoholic or other liver disease can over-respond, which may hide pancreatic disease. A weak response can follow vagotomy (surgery cutting the vagus nerve), inflammatory bowel disease or anticholinergic medicines. Acid-reducing drugs, including proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers, can raise gastrin and falsely suggest a gastrinoma, so they are usually stopped before testing [1].

No, according to the trials. In 1998, publicity about a child with autism who seemed to improve after a single secretin dose led thousands of families to seek it [5][6]. A 1999 double-blind trial in 60 children found no significant improvement on any measure after a single dose compared with saline [5].

A Cochrane systematic review later pooled 16 randomized trials involving more than 900 children. It found consistent results showing no improvement in the core features of autism with single or multiple doses, and concluded secretin should not be given as an autism treatment [6].
